rv.q: Fat Ham is a riot of a play that manages to be both hilarious and deeply moving.
For me, seeing “Fat Ham,” even multiple times, thus remains a revelation and a balm.
Not to mention that "Fat Ham" is a total gas — the funniest and most invigorating new show on Broadway
James Ijames has created a brilliant contemporary riff on 'Hamlet' that crackles with wit, wisdom and emotional truth.
By turns sweet and saucy (and very funny), the play stays just close enough to Hamlet to keep us off-balance.
At no point does this play feel like anything other than a big-fun Broadway show: it’s a smart, fearless and often wildly entertaining 90 minutes, filled with radical ideas and absurdist spectacle.
Ali’s direction, Fat Ham is an exhilarating example of Ijames’s world-building, his prowess for merriment and lyrical musing.

James Ijames' Pulitzer Prize-winning play 'Fat Ham' is a raucous, irreverent and ultimately moving riff on 'Hamlet' that brings Shakespeare's tragedy into a contemporary Black family's backyard barbecue.
The brash and bold production reminded me of the scholar Zandria Robinson's recent observation about the South being the home of all things queer and non-normative.
Fat Ham serves an endless tray of delight but every bit of sparkle added ironically dulls the play's brilliance.
The play is at its best when it lets its characters be messy and human, rather than symbolic vessels for larger ideas about Black masculinity and family trauma.
Instead, we get that splashy finale complete with a confetti cannon — played as celebratory, though the insistence on joy comes off as condescending.

Conceptually, I’m right there with what Ijames is cooking up, but by the time that finale came around, I was left a little cold, craving some pulled pork but, instead, getting a takeout sandwich encased in too many layers of cling wrap.
Much of Ijames’ “Fat Ham” is playful ideas that don’t add up.
The ensemble is as fabulous as ever.
Without apologies to the purists, it is a modern classic in its own right.
“Fat Ham” is the most fun you’ll have at any play this Broadway season.

So it is nothing short of miraculous that James Ijames’s Fat Ham, winner of the 2022. Pulitzer Prize, not only holds up to that comparison, it manages to explore and amplify Shakespeare’s classic and to stand on its own as a wholly original piece of theater.
Change is possible; we just must want to do it.
Just be careful you don’t die laughing while watching it.
You can't help but feel welcome, drawn in, and caught up in the story.
It's scrumptious and utterly satisfying.

Simply put, for Ijames’ insightfully idiosyncratic take on Hamlet, we’re not in Elsinore anymore, and that’s a good thing.
Fat Ham is scrumptuously satiating now, meatier and far more meaningful than it was in its off-Broadway incarnation.
Ijames' characters are as American as pulled pork and baby back ribs, which emphasizes the universality of Shakespeare's work.

As led by an excellent ensemble cast, the solid production (directed by Saheem Ali) successfully balances the play’s intimate emotional moments, terrific stagecraft (including surprise entrances and exits by the ghost) and far-out comedy.

He also delivers what is perhaps the single most memorable moment in “Fat Ham,” a long soliloquy (very much not Shakespearean) about a dream encounter that climaxes in, um, sexual congress with a gingerbread man cookie.
For his part, Marcel Spears as Juicy might bring to mind another Black, hefty, gay, and moody character, namely Usher from Michael R. Jackson's A Strange Loop.

Shakespeare is the indisputable dominating figure on stages around the world—delivered in many languages. But, no where does he seem to get more nuanced interpretations than in hometown New York City. This more recent example is a move from Theatre to Broadway in an unconventional spin on the Danish play called “Fat Ham.
It takes that play, messes with it, f**ks it up the ass, and soars.

cn.t: Critics praise this Pulitzer-winning Hamlet adaptation as audacious, hilarious, and tenderhearted, with strong performances and a fresh take on masculinity and violence set at a Southern barbecue, though some find it overly broad or distanced.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
